title: Stars trails over Armazones
caption: Star trails around the south celestial pole over Cerro Armazones, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at the ELT site, Cerro Armazones, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Stars trace dotted circles around a point near the centre of this image, taken from the summit of Cerro Armazones. That point is the south celestial pole. The mountain, 3046 metres high, was chosen as the site of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope.

The picture combines multiple exposures. As Earth rotates, the whole night sky appears to turn around the southern celestial pole, and each star moves a little between frames. Stacked together, the frames turn every star into a line of dots curving around the centre.

Two pieces of equipment appear in the frame. The instrument on the right, the Differential Image Motion Monitor or DIMM, measures atmospheric seeing: how much turbulence in the air blurs the view. To its left rises a white and red tower that serves as the meteorological station. Together they gathered the kind of information needed to judge whether the summit would suit a giant telescope.

understand.summary: This is a stack of night-time photographs taken in visible light with a camera on Cerro Armazones. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points; only by combining many exposures can a camera record their slow circling of the pole.

behind.observatory: the ELT site, Cerro Armazones, Chile
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Stars close to the pole trace small, tight circles, while those farther away sweep out wide arcs, so the pattern of trails is a kind of map of the sky's rotation.
alt: Dotted star trails circling a point near the centre of the sky, with an instrument on the right and a white and red tower to its left.
